metadata.title: Programming semantics for multiprogrammed computations
metadata.abstract_summary: A shared multiprogrammed computation needs an addressing scheme where access to any resource is mediated by an unforgeable "capability" naming both the resource and the operations permitted on it, rather than by a global namespace checked against an access-control list - the origin of capability-based addressing.

sections.heading: Claims
sections.text:
As the authors state it:

> The semantics are defined for a number of meta-instructions which perform operations essential to the writing of programs in multiprogrammed computer systems. These meta-instructions relate to parallel processing, protecting of separate computations, program debugging, and the sharing among users of memory segments and other computing objects, the names of which are hierarchically structured. The language sophistication contemplated is midway between an assembly language and an advanced algebraic language.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: A formal and conceptual systems-design paper: defines the capability abstraction, sketches how a supervisor/kernel would create, pass, and revoke capabilities, and argues this gives protection without the coordination overhead of a centralized permission table.

sections.heading: Evidence & Limits
sections.text:
- A design proposal, not an implementation study - no built system or benchmark appears in this 1966 paper.
- Capability-based addressing was subsequently built (the Cambridge CAP computer, later object-capability languages, seL4, and current object-capability security research) validating the idea over six decades, but the specific mechanisms sketched here were substantially refined by that later work.
- The root of a lineage this catalogue's own `librarian/policy.py` sits in a different branch of: a closed, named action registry rather than an unforgeable per-grant token, worth reading against directly.
